e.t: This word means “birthright,” referring to the special inheritance or family standing associated with being born first. It can be spoken of as something a person possesses, gives, receives, or loses. Scripture uses it in discussions of Esau and Jacob, and also when describing the rights or status connected with a firstborn son. In this Hebrew corpus, the word occurs 14 times, chiefly in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and 1 Chronicles. Its central idea is an inherited firstborn privilege that may be transferred or assigned.

Bered is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Bered” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a person or place in the Old Testament, and its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage. This name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. The available passages preserve it as a name, not as a stated action, quality, or theological concept.

This Hebrew noun refers to “deeds”: what a person has done or carries out. It names deeds as a subject being considered, spoken of, or connected with what follows in a sentence. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, once each in 2 Samuel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “treasure.” It functions as a naming word for something stored or held in a treasury. It occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in Ezra. The term appears in passages concerning royal records and resources connected with the temple, but its precise role in each verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense remains consistent: treasure is something kept and valued.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “David,” referring to the biblical king and the person connected with his family line. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. The name appears 1,031 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Ruth 4:17 and continuing through Zechariah 13:1. Scripture frequently presents David as a central figure in Israel’s history, with references involving leadership, speech, giving, commands, death, and God’s dealings with him.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the Hagarites, also rendered “Hagrites,” a named people group mentioned in the Old Testament. It functions as a designation rather than a description of an action or quality. The word occurs six times, all in the Old Testament, especially in 1 Chronicles and once in Psalm 83. Its references place the Hagarites among peoples involved in conflict and other recorded events, but the word itself primarily identifies them.

This Hebrew word means “fool” and describes a person regarded as foolish. It functions as a person-description rather than naming an action, object, or place. The word occurs 26 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with most occurrences in Proverbs, where such person-descriptions are especially common. Its basic meaning remains consistent across its uses, while the surrounding verse determines the particular force of calling someone a fool.

This Hebrew word is a pronoun meaning “they,” referring to more than one person or thing. It points back to people, objects, or groups already identified in the sentence or surrounding passage, rather than naming them again. Its meaning is relational: the reader understands whom it refers to from the context. It occurs 566 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a commonly used way to refer to multiple subjects or objects. The precise referent changes from passage to passage.

This Hebrew word means “cause.” It functions as a term identifying what brings about an event or provides the grounds for it. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezekiel 24:26. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the immediate context, but its basic sense is a cause connected with something that happens or is stated.

e.t: In the Hebrew Old Testament, this noun means “iniquity.” It is used to speak of iniquity as something associated with people, their speech, and their actions. The word occurs 79 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with occurrences in Psalms, Job, Isaiah, and Proverbs. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. The surrounding context shows how it functions there.

“Abi” is a personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 18:2. The available English rendering preserves it as “Abi,” so its ordinary meaning here is the person’s name itself, not a broader vocabulary concept. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that individual’s specific role or significance in the passage.

This Hebrew word expresses the relation of being “beside.” It functions as a relational term, showing that one person or thing is positioned beside another, or is treated as beside it within the sentence. It appears 16 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, making it a recurring term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and the relationship the sentence establishes.

This Hebrew word means “extinct.” It describes the condition of something that has reached extinction, functioning as a word of description rather than a name for a person or place. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Job 17:1. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this basic lexical meaning.

e.t: This word means "outside" and functions as a term marking a location beyond an inner place, boundary, or enclosed area. It can describe where something is situated or where an action takes place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 164 times, showing that it is a broadly used word for distinguishing what is beyond or apart from an interior space. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the place or boundary being discussed.

This Hebrew word refers to “bulwarks,” strong defensive works built as part of a city’s protection. It functions as a plural noun, naming such fortifications rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 48:13, so its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. Its repeated English rendering as “bulwarks” supports this basic sense.

The name appears 13 times in the Hebrew corpus, all within 1 Samuel 1–2. Its recorded uses connect Hannah with speech, worship, and the birth of a son, so readers should understand it primarily as a person’s name. The surrounding passage is needed to understand what Hannah is doing or saying in any particular verse.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “sword,” naming a weapon used for fighting, killing, and defense. It commonly refers to a literal blade, while its surrounding scriptural use can connect it with battle, death, commands to destroy, and the giving or carrying of weapons. It appears 413 times in the Hebrew Bible, so it is a broad and recurring word rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew verb means “dip”: to put or immerse something into a liquid or substance. It describes an action performed with an object, such as dipping something into blood, water, or another material. The word occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent action rather than an abstract idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being dipped and what substance receives it.

Ahinadab is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:14, and is rendered as “Ahinadab.” Because the available information identifies the word as a name but does not provide a separate definition, its primary function is to identify this individual. The surrounding verse supplies the specific details about him.

This Hebrew word refers to a “basket.” It names a physical container and functions as a noun in its four Old Testament occurrences, all found in Deuteronomy. The word appears in Deuteronomy 26:2 and 26:4, and again in Deuteronomy 28:5 and 28:17. Its straightforward meaning remains “basket”; the surrounding verse determines what is placed in it or what happens to it.

Jehieli is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Jehieli” in English. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles 26:21–22. Because no explanatory gloss or definition is preserved for it, the name itself is the supported meaning; its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a place named “Jearim.” It functions as a proper place-name rather than a general description or action. The name appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 15:10, and the English renderings preserve it as “Jearim.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise geographical or contextual role cannot be explained further from this word alone.

e.t: “Oil” is a noun naming a substance spoken of as something that can be given, possessed, or received. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs 23 times, including passages about offerings, provisions, abundance, and promised blessing. It can also appear in speech describing what people may enjoy in a prosperous land. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Jakim is a Hebrew personal name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament record, it is rendered consistently as “Jakim” and occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. Readers should therefore understand it as identifying an individual rather than as a general instruction or theological term. The name itself is not given an explained definition here, so its supported meaning is its use as a person’s name.

This Hebrew word means “belly,” referring to the front or inner bodily area. It functions as a noun, naming a physical part of the body rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 51:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is the bodily term “belly.”

This Hebrew word means “weary,” describing someone or something worn down, exhausted, or no longer able to continue easily. It is used in the Old Testament across 19 occurrences, including descriptions of people who are burdened or faint and conditions that become exhausting. As a predicate, it states that the subject has become weary or is experiencing weariness. The surrounding verse determines whether the weariness is physical, emotional, or connected with an ongoing situation.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to need, want, or poverty—the condition of lacking what is necessary. It can describe material shortage and the absence of needed resources. In the Old Testament, it appears 13 times, including passages about supplying another person’s need and warnings associated with poverty. Its common renderings include “want” and “poverty,” showing how the same basic idea may be expressed as either lacking something or living in needy circumstances.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “bitterness.” It names the quality or experience of what is bitter, serving as a noun rather than describing an action or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs once, in Job 9:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its basic lexical sense is clear: bitterness. This word therefore points to something bitter as an experienced or expressed reality.

The Hebrew word means “rule,” describing the presence or exercise of governing power. It functions as a term for rule itself, rather than naming a person who rules or a specific act of ruling. In this Hebrew corpus it occurs once, in Proverbs 25:28. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and comparison with the other words in that sentence.

This Hebrew word means “idol,” referring to an object of worship that is not the living God. It occurs four times in the Old Testament corpus, in two verses: 1 Kings 15:13 and 2 Chronicles 15:16. Its limited use points to a specific term for an idol rather than a broad word for every form of false worship. The surrounding passage supplies the particular significance in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “banquet.” It is a noun used to name such an occasion rather than to describe an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 6:7. The available wording supports the basic sense of a banquet, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what this particular banquet represents or how it functions there.

This is a Hebrew word and should be understood within the Hebrew Old Testament corpus.

The word occurs 29 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring connection between separation, purity, and obedience to God’s commands. e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a habitation: a place where people or creatures live. It normally identifies a settled living place rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 35 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is used across a range of passages concerning places of residence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Naham is a personal name, rather than a word whose ordinary meaning is supplied here as an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Hebrew text and occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:19. Because the available rendering preserves the name as “Naham” and no short definition is provided, the name itself is the clearest supported explanation; its particular significance depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Hebrew word means “haft,” referring to a specific part associated with a sword. It occurs once in the Old Testament, in Judges 3:22. In that occurrence, it functions as the object connected with actions of entering, coming out, being closed, and being seized. Thus, the word identifies a tangible part of the sword rather than an action, quality, or person.

The Hebrew word means “mighty.” It functions as an adjective describing someone or something marked by exceptional strength or power. In its six occurrences in the Hebrew Old Testament, it is applied in settings involving people and forces. The word therefore points to ability, force, or capacity that is beyond ordinary measure, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

This Hebrew word means “indeed,” an emphatic expression used to affirm or reinforce a statement. It functions as a brief word of emphasis rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Genesis and Joshua. Its basic force is to mark what is being said as firmly true; the surrounding verse determines the specific statement it emphasizes.

This Hebrew noun means “secret.” It names a matter that is not openly known but is kept within a private setting or shared with selected people. In the Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, showing a recurring use for something held from public view. The surrounding verse determines whether the secret belongs to people, is shared among them, or is made known by God.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “valued”—treated as precious or worth much. It functions in sentences to describe the worth assigned to something, rather than naming the object itself. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it is rendered “valued” three times, showing that this is the clearest supported sense. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Sered is a personal name, rendered as “Sered,” rather than a descriptive word with a separate stated meaning. It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears twice in that corpus, once in Genesis 46:14 and once in Numbers 26:26. Because no broader definition or descriptive use is provided, the clearest understanding is simply the name itself. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

e.t: “Uzzi” is a personal name used for several men in the Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than as a common noun or action word, so its role in a sentence is to identify a particular person. This Hebrew name appears 11 times, especially in genealogical records in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name itself does not identify one single individual; the surrounding verse distinguishes which Uzzi is intended.

Ilai is a personal name, preserved in English as “Ilai.” It functions as the name of an individual rather than as a general description, action, or quality. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:29. Because no lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, its personal-name function is clear, while a more specific meaning or significance should not be inferred from the name alone.

This Hebrew word means “wearied,” describing someone or something as being in a state of weariness. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Jeremiah 4:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the condition of being wearied.

This Hebrew word is represented by “that” and functions as a connecting word within its sentence. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Micah. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise grammatical role can vary with the sentence in which it occurs. Its occurrences include Job 9:20, Proverbs 10:9 and 28:18, Isaiah 59:8, and Micah 3:9.

“Now” means “now,” pointing to the present moment or the immediate situation in view. It is a Hebrew adverb, so it commonly marks when something is happening, being said, or becoming relevant. This word occurs 435 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi, showing that it serves ordinary time-related statements across many kinds of passages. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding words and sentence.

This Hebrew word means “fine,” functioning as a descriptive word for something presented as especially valuable or excellent. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, often describing precious or desirable things. Its uses include references to gold, commandments, and other objects of high worth, showing that “fine” can describe both material treasures and things greatly prized. The word appears from Job through Lamentations, with several occurrences in Psalms. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. No clear meaning phrase or translation term is available for this Hebrew word. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nehemiah 10:24, but the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here. Therefore, its precise meaning cannot be stated more specifically without adding information Scripture itself has not provided in this context.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses “open,” functioning as a noun-like term that names an open condition or reality. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel. Its use is connected with what is open in relation to speech and with a giving event. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains “open.”

The word refers to “burning,” functioning as a naming term for a fiery or inflamed condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Leviticus 13 and once in Proverbs 16. Its uses therefore range from a condition considered in skin examination to an image associated with destructive fire. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains something burning or producing fiery harm.

e.t: Kidron is the name of a specific place in the Hebrew Scriptures. It functions as a proper name, so it identifies that place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 11 times in the Old Testament, across 10 verses, and is consistently rendered “Kidron.” Its use appears in accounts involving David, Israel’s kings, and events connected with removing objects associated with false worship. The surrounding verse determines what is happening at Kidron in each passage.

This Hebrew word is a place name, referring to a town called “Kirjathbaal” and rendered “Baal” in another English translation. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in two verses in Joshua: Joshua 15:60 and Joshua 18:14. The name identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical evidence supports understanding it as the name of this particular town.

This Hebrew word means “far.” It functions as a descriptive word, indicating distance rather than nearness. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Ezra 6:6. Because the word occurs only once and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the context. Its central idea remains straightforward: it identifies something as far away or at a considerable distance.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “spit,” referring to what is expelled from the mouth. It functions as a noun describing a physical substance. It occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus: twice in Job and once in Isaiah. Its uses are connected with an object being acted upon or given, but the precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word refers to preparing or working with “spices,” especially in making fragrant substances such as perfume, ointment, or incense. It can describe the skilled activity involved in combining aromatic materials, rather than merely naming a single spice. In the Old Testament, it appears eight times, including descriptions of sacred perfume and fragrant preparations, as well as spices used with burial. Its exact nuance depends on whether the sentence emphasizes the materials or the preparation of them.

This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of what is “left.” It describes a person, thing, or group that continues after others have been removed, gone, or lost. In a sentence, it functions as the action or state assigned to the subject, indicating what has been left in place or continues to be present. It occurs 133 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is used broadly for situations involving survival, preservation, or what remains after a separating event.

e.t: Ararat is a geographic name identifying a location. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, always referring to Ararat rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name occurs in Genesis 8:4 and later in 2 Kings 19:37, Isaiah 37:38, and Jeremiah 51:27. Its use in the two parallel accounts connected with worship or bowing confirms that it functions as the place named in those passages. The precise significance of the location in any one verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “coal,” the dark, combustible material associated with burning heat. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Lamentations 4:8. The available rendering supports the basic meaning “coal,” but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the image functions in that passage. As a noun referring to a material, it names the substance itself rather than an action or quality.

This Hebrew word refers to “pits”—hollow places that can serve as concealed traps or places of danger. It occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, appearing in two Psalms and once in Jeremiah. Its uses are associated with pits set before or around people, so the word points to a physical hazard rather than an abstract idea. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is a pit or trap-like hollow.

This Hebrew word describes ease, referring to a condition in which a person or people are free from distress or pressure. It is used as a descriptive word for settled circumstances rather than as an action. In the Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including passages in Job, Psalms, Jeremiah, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: It means “sleep,” referring to the ordinary condition of being asleep. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is used for sleep as a human experience and as a condition that may come, be interrupted, or be absent. The word occurs 23 times in 23 verses, from Genesis through Zechariah. It can be spoken of directly or connected with what someone does. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 7:3. The available information identifies the Hebrew word but does not provide a clear English gloss or short definition. Therefore, its precise ordinary meaning cannot be stated confidently apart from the wording and surrounding passage of that verse. The reference locates its sole occurrence, while the word’s identity confirms that it is a distinct Hebrew term rather than a New Testament Greek word.

This Hebrew word means “six,” identifying a quantity of six. It functions as a number used to count or describe something that totals six. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Ezra and once in Daniel. It does not by itself name the object, person, or measurement being counted; the surrounding wording determines that. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears: it marks the total of six.

In the Old Testament, it occurs 20 times and is used for something presented as a model or likeness. Its normal sense points to an observable arrangement rather than an abstract idea. The surrounding verse determines what the pattern represents or how it is used.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “badgers,” especially in passages describing material used for coverings and tabernacle furnishings. It appears 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, primarily in Exodus and Numbers, with one later occurrence in Ezekiel. The word functions as a noun naming the animal or its hide, and Scripture repeatedly connects it with coverings, skins, or items given for sacred use. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word can mean “fashion” or “store,” depending on how it functions in the sentence. It appears twice in the Old Testament: once in Ezekiel 43:11 and once in Nahum 2:9. In Ezekiel it is rendered “fashion,” while in Nahum it is rendered “store.” Thus, the word can describe an arranged form or something kept in reserve, but the surrounding verse determines which sense is intended.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 49:7. Because the surrounding verse text and an explicit definition are not available here, its precise English meaning cannot be stated responsibly beyond this context-sensitive description. The word functions as part of the statement in that verse, and its full force must be understood from the words around it rather than from the word alone.
